planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in a sheltered site with sharply drained, lean soil in partial shade to full sun; give it protection from cold winds and mulch the root zone the first winter or two while it establishes.

directions: Native to the eastern Himalaya and Yunnan, Griffith's plumbago is a wiry, loosely branched, semi-evergreen shrub whose reddish stems and oval, slightly toothed leaves persist through mild winters before dropping in harder cold. From late summer into the first frosts it produces clusters of intense deep-blue flowers at the branch tips, a color that intensifies as the surrounding foliage shifts to flame-red and burgundy in autumn, so flowers and fall color overlap for several weeks. It wants sharply drained, lean soil and a sheltered position, since it is less cold-hardy than the related Ceratostigma plumbaginoides and willmottianum and appreciates protection from harsh winter wind. Once settled it is quite drought-tolerant and needs only an annual tidy-up of dead or frost-damaged wood in spring.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society - Ceratostigma griffithii

planting.note: Plant in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun with some shelter from cold wind; cut all stems back hard to a few inches above ground in early spring since flowers form on new wood.

directions: 'Forest Blue' is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit selection of Chinese plumbago, bred for a noticeably more compact, densely branching habit than the species while keeping its best qualities intact. Wiry, red-tinted stems carry clusters of brilliant cobalt-blue flowers from midsummer through October, timed to overlap with a fall foliage display in which the green leaves turn fiery orange and red. Because it dies back to the base in cold winters in the northern part of its range, it is best treated as a woody perennial there and cut to the ground each spring to renew growth, while in milder zones it holds a low semi-shrubby framework year-round. Its tighter, twiggier growth makes it easier to fit into small borders and gravel gardens than the looser species form.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs 4 to 8 inches apart in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; keep evenly moist until the clumps knit together into a solid mat.

directions: Silver Dragon is a variegated selection of the common dwarf mondo grass, with tough, grass-like blades in a grayer green than the species, streaked lengthwise with crisp silvery white. Short summer spikes of small white to lilac-tinged, bell-shaped flowers are followed by round blue-black berries, though the plant is grown almost entirely for its evergreen, fine-textured foliage rather than its bloom. It spreads slowly by rhizomes into a dense, weed-suppressing turf and tolerates deep shade and root competition better than most true grasses, making it a useful pale accent to break up plantings of plain green mondo or liriope beneath trees. Established plantings shrug off both summer heat and brief dry spells, though color and vigor are best with consistent moisture.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society - Ophiopogon japonicus 'Silver Dragon'

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, allowing more room between plants than for standard black mondo since Black Beard forms noticeably larger, fuller clumps.

directions: Black Beard (patented as 'Yapard', US PP22,128) is a distinct selection of black mondo grass bred over decades in Cornwall, England, chosen for taller, fuller, more vigorous clumps than the widely grown 'Nigrescens'. New foliage emerges deep green and quickly darkens to near-black, strap-like blades reaching roughly a foot tall, well above the typical 6-to-8-inch height of standard black mondo. Small pinkish-white summer flowers are followed by glossy black berries, and the clumps thicken steadily by short stolons into a dense, near-black carpet under trees or along shaded path edges. It accepts more sun than most Ophiopogon selections if soil moisture is kept consistent, but colors darkest and grows best in partial to full shade.
sources: US Plant Patent PP22,128 - Ophiopogon plant named 'Yapard'

planting.note: Plant container-grown clumps in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; since Ruscus is typically dioecious, grow at least one male and one female plant nearby if berries are wanted.

directions: Native to Iberia and northwest Africa, spineless butcher's broom forms upright, unbranched clumps of broad, glossy, dark-green cladodes (flattened leaf-like stems) that lack the stiff spine tip of its well-known relative Ruscus aculeatus, making it far more pleasant to handle and site near paths. Its species name refers to an unusual trait: tiny white flowers, and later red berries on female plants, are produced directly from the underside of each cladode rather than from separate stems. It spreads slowly by rhizomes into a dense, weed-suppressing clump and is remarkably tolerant of deep shade, dry soil, and root competition beneath established trees, conditions where few other broadleaf evergreens perform. Long used by florists for its durable cut foliage, it is equally valuable in the shade garden as a tough, low-maintenance textural evergreen.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society - Ruscus hypophyllum
Plants for a Future (pfaf.org) - Ruscus hypophyllum
Plant Delights Nursery catalog

planting.note: Plant container-grown clumps in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade and be patient; this hybrid butcher's broom is exceptionally slow-growing and best used where a small, permanent evergreen accent is wanted rather than fast coverage.

directions: Ruscus x microglossus is a naturally occurring hybrid between Ruscus hypoglossum and Ruscus hypophyllum, combining the soft, spineless, thumb-sized cladodes of both parents on low, arching stems under a foot and a half tall. Tiny flowers and, on fertilized female plants, small berries appear directly from the center of each flattened cladode in late winter, a curious detail shared with its parent species. It is extraordinarily slow to spread, sometimes taking two decades to form a clump two feet across, but that same trait makes it a long-lived, essentially maintenance-free evergreen for the deepest, driest shade under trees where almost nothing else will grow. Best reserved for a permanent spot as a specimen or small-scale groundcover in a shaded woodland or courtyard garden rather than for quick coverage.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society - Ruscus x microglossus

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this low, wide-spreading selection is grown as a groundcover conifer rather than a specimen shrub, so give it room to spread outward.

directions: Gold Splash is a low, wide-spreading, prostrate selection of Japanese plum yew notable for holding bright golden-yellow needle color even in fairly deep shade, unlike most golden conifers, which need strong sun to color well and often revert to green in shade. Slow-growing at only a few inches a year, it forms a dense, horizontally layered mat of foliage that works well as a textural, color-contrasting groundcover beneath high tree canopy or spilling over a low wall. Like other plum yews it is untouched by deer, tolerant of both moist and moderately dry shaded soils, and essentially free of significant pests or diseases once established. Its combination of deep-shade tolerance, gold color, and spreading habit fills a niche few other evergreen groundcover conifers can match.
sources: Oregon State University Landscape Plants database - Cephalotaxus harringtonia 'Gold Splash'
